# The optical module and the observable {#sec-optical-module}

## The physical question {#sec-optical-module-question}

@sec-spectral-rte gives the spectral intensity $I_\lambda(\mathbf x,\hat s,t)$
everywhere. A module sits at one of those points. That is not yet a signal, and
the gap between the two is what this chapter closes.

Four things stand between the field and the count. Light arrives at the module
from many directions at once, and a module is not equally sensitive to all of
them: a photon that comes in along the axis and one that comes in from behind
are not worth the same. Sensitivity also depends on wavelength, through the
quantum efficiency of the photocathode and through the transmission of
everything the light crosses on the way in. An intensity is a flux per unit
area, so an area is needed to turn it into a number of photons at all. And the
answer is a count of *photoelectrons*, not of photons, because only a fraction
of the arriving light is converted.

The output of this chapter is therefore a definite number for each module and
each time bin, together with an honest statement of what has been modelled and
what has been left out. What is left out is everything downstream of the
photocathode: there is no trigger here, no single-photoelectron charge
distribution, no saturation and no noise. The quantity computed is an
expectation, the mean over photon histories, and a readout simulation is what
turns such an expectation into counts with fluctuations.

## Assumptions and definitions {#sec-optical-module-assumptions}

A module in LightHit is a **point** carrying three response factors. It has no
surface, so no photon is traced to a spot on a glass sphere and no ray is
refracted at the glass. For module $d$:

| Symbol | Meaning | Units |
|:--|:--|:--|
| $\mathbf x_d$ | position of the module | $\mathrm m$ |
| $S_d$ | reference collecting area | $\mathrm m^2$ |
| $\epsilon(\lambda)$ | spectral efficiency | dimensionless |
| $\mathcal A(c)$ | angular acceptance | dimensionless |
| $\hat{\mathbf o}_d$ | stored orientation | dimensionless |
| $\hat{\mathbf n}_d=-\hat{\mathbf o}_d$ | travel direction of a head-on photon | dimensionless |
| $\hat{\mathbf s}$ | direction in which an incident photon travels | dimensionless |
| $c=\hat{\mathbf s}\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}_d$ | acceptance argument | dimensionless |

The phrase *arrival direction* is avoided throughout, because it is ambiguous:
it can mean the direction a photon travels or the direction from the module
towards where the photon came from, and those differ by a sign. This chapter
says **travel direction** for $\hat{\mathbf s}$ and **direction towards the
source** for its negative, and never abbreviates either.

The response is modelled as a product of three independent factors,
$$
\text{response}=S_d\times\epsilon(\lambda)\times\mathcal A(c),
$$ {#eq-module-factorisation}
and each factor is worth a paragraph of its own, because the contract that the
code enforces on each one is different.

**The area.** $S_d$ is a reference collecting area in square metres, stored per
module, and it may differ between modules of one array. It is the factor that
carries the dimension; the other two are pure numbers. It is *not* the surface
area of a sphere and no geometrical projection is applied to it: a point
detector has no cross-section that varies with incidence angle, and whatever
angular variation a real module has belongs in $\mathcal A$.

**The spectral efficiency.** $\epsilon(\lambda)$ collects every dimensionless
wavelength-dependent factor the user wants to apply --- quantum efficiency, the
transmission of the glass, the transmission of the gel, anything else. The
package fixes no value for it. The contract requires only that it return finite
non-negative numbers; it is **not** constrained to lie in $[0,1]$, so it is not
a probability unless the user chose to make it one. A calibration scale folded
into $\epsilon$ is legitimate and the code will not object.

**The angular acceptance.** $\mathcal A(c)$ is finite and non-negative and
depends on the direction only through the single cosine $c$, so the module is
axially symmetric about $\hat{\mathbf n}_d$. The convention recommended here is
$$
\mathcal A(+1)=1,
$$ {#eq-acceptance-normalisation}
with the absolute scale kept in $S_d\epsilon$. The code does not impose this.
Nothing stops a user from putting the same factor of two into $S_d$ and into
the peak of $\mathcal A$, and the result will be four times the intended
signal with no error raised anywhere. @eq-module-factorisation is a product of
three numbers, and which of them carries the overall normalisation is a
decision the user must make once and keep.

### Orientation and the sign {#sec-optical-module-orientation}

`DetectorArray` stores $\hat{\mathbf o}_d$, the direction pointing **from** the
module **towards** the hemisphere it accepts: a module aimed at a source has
$\hat{\mathbf o}_d$ pointing at the source. A photon from that source travels
the other way, from the source to the module, so its travel direction is
$$
\hat{\mathbf n}_d=-\,\hat{\mathbf o}_d,
$$ {#eq-module-orientation}
and the acceptance argument for a photon travelling along $\hat{\mathbf s}$ is
$$
c=\hat{\mathbf s}\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}_d=-\,\hat{\mathbf s}\cdot\hat{\mathbf o}_d .
$$ {#eq-module-cosine}
For a point source at $\mathbf x_{\rm src}$ the photon that reaches the module
without scattering travels along
$\hat{\mathbf s}=(\mathbf x_d-\mathbf x_{\rm src})/|\mathbf x_d-\mathbf x_{\rm src}|$,
and substituting into @eq-module-cosine gives the equivalent form
$$
c=\hat{\mathbf o}_d\cdot
\frac{\mathbf x_{\rm src}-\mathbf x_d}{|\mathbf x_{\rm src}-\mathbf x_d|},
$$ {#eq-module-head-on-cosine}
which is what `DetectorArray.head_on_cosine` computes: the cosine between the
stored orientation and the direction from the module towards the source. The
two minus signs cancel, and that cancellation is the entire content of the
convention.

Three cases fix it beyond argument. A module looking straight at the source has
$c=+1$ and sees $\mathcal A(+1)$. A module whose axis is perpendicular to the
line joining it to the source has $c=0$. A module looking directly away has
$c=-1$. @sec-optical-module-example measures all three.

## Derivation {#sec-optical-module-derivation}

The rate at which module $d$ produces photoelectrons is
@eq-module-factorisation applied to the incident intensity and integrated over
everything the module cannot distinguish --- direction and wavelength:
$$
R_d(t)=S_d\int\mathrm d\lambda\;\epsilon(\lambda)
\int_{S^2}\mathrm d\hat{\mathbf s}\;
\mathcal A(\hat{\mathbf s}\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}_d)\,
I_\lambda(\mathbf x_d,\hat{\mathbf s},t).
$$ {#eq-module-rate}
The units cancel as they must: $\mathrm m^2$ from $S_d$, $\mathrm{nm}$ from
$\mathrm d\lambda$ and $\mathrm{sr}$ from $\mathrm d\hat{\mathbf s}$ consume
three of the four units of $I_\lambda$, leaving $\mathrm{ns}^{-1}$, and the two
dimensionless factors change nothing. $R_d$ is a rate of photoelectrons per
nanosecond, and it is an expectation, not a realisation.

Integrating over a bin gives the observable of @eq-overview-pe,
$$
N_{db}=\int_{t_b}^{t_{b+1}}R_d(t)\,\mathrm dt ,
$$ {#eq-module-bin}
and over all time the integrated charge
$$
Q_d=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}R_d(t)\,\mathrm dt .
$$ {#eq-module-charge}

The distinction drawn at @eq-overview-charge is worth repeating here in the
module's own terms, because this is the chapter where both quantities are
defined. `TransportResponse.charge_pe` is @eq-module-charge, evaluated at zero
frequency; `TransportResponse.bins_pe` is @eq-module-bin for a finite list of
bins. The sum of the bins is **not** required to equal the charge, and in
general does not: the window is finite, and the inversion that produces the
bins is not exact. Where a total is wanted, @eq-module-charge is the quantity
to read.

### The acceptance as a Legendre series {#sec-optical-module-legendre}

Because $\mathcal A$ depends on one cosine only, it has a Legendre expansion,
and the coefficients
$$
\alpha_\ell=2\pi\int_{-1}^{1}\mathcal A(c)\,P_\ell(c)\,\mathrm dc
$$ {#eq-acceptance-coefficients}
reconstruct it through
$$
\mathcal A(c)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\frac{2\ell+1}{4\pi}\,
\alpha_\ell P_\ell(c).
$$ {#eq-acceptance-series}
The normalisation is fixed by the isotropic limit. A module that accepts every
direction with unit efficiency has $\mathcal A\equiv1$, and then
$$
\alpha_0=2\pi\int_{-1}^{1}\mathrm dc=4\pi,\qquad \alpha_{\ell>0}=0 ,
$$ {#eq-acceptance-isotropic}
which is the convention the package uses: $\alpha_0=4\pi$ for a perfectly
isotropic, fully efficient receiver, so that the directional module reduces to
the isotropic one by a single coefficient.

The **acceptance bandwidth** $L_A$ is the largest degree whose coefficient is
still significant. Three cases behave differently and all three occur in
practice. A polynomial acceptance of degree $p$ has $\alpha_\ell=0$ exactly for
$\ell>p$, so $L_A=p$ and the series is a finite sum. A smooth but
non-polynomial acceptance has an infinite tail whose coefficients decay fast,
so a truncation is an approximation with a measurable error. A response built
by clipping at zero *inside* the interval --- the common `max(..., 0)` idiom ---
has a kink, and the coefficients of a function with a discontinuous derivative
decay only algebraically: the series never terminates, and no finite degree
represents it exactly.

The package measures which case it is in rather than assuming. It never
declares a clipped response band-limited: it reports the largest degree still
above tolerance inside a probed range, and when that degree saturates the
range, that is the answer --- the response is not band-limited there, and a
truncation has to be chosen deliberately and its residual read. One caution
about reading the report: when the bandwidth saturates the probe there is
nothing above it left to measure, so the reported residual is zero and means
nothing at all. The number to look at in that case is the size of the
coefficients themselves at high degree.

Why the bandwidth matters at all belongs to @sec-directional-om, where the
acceptance enters the angular contraction for scattered light and $L_A$ sets
how much of that contraction has to be carried. Nothing about that machinery is
needed here.

### The centroid cosine is not a directional response {#sec-optical-module-centroid}

`DetectorArray.angular_weight(source_position)` evaluates $\mathcal A$ at the
single cosine @eq-module-head-on-cosine. It is exact for what it describes: a
photon that travels in a straight line from that point to the module. It is the
right quantity for the unscattered term, and it is a legitimate quick geometric
estimate.

It is **not** the response of a module to scattered light. Scattered light
arrives at the module from a distribution of travel directions, and
@eq-module-rate keeps $\mathcal A$ *inside* the integral over
$\hat{\mathbf s}$ for exactly that reason. Replacing the integral by
$\mathcal A$ evaluated at one direction --- the direction of the source, or of
the centroid of an extended event --- is an approximation whose error is not
controlled by anything in this chapter. It is not how the production route
computes a directional module; @sec-directional-om is.

### What the array shares {#sec-optical-module-shared}

`DetectorArray` lets every module differ in position, in orientation, in
reference area and in its identifiers. It does not let them differ in the
*shape* of the response: `angular_acceptance` and `spectral_efficiency` are one
callable each, shared by every module in the array. An array of modules with
genuinely different angular shapes or different photocathode efficiencies
cannot be expressed as a single `DetectorArray` today. It has to be split into
several arrays, or the contract has to be extended to accept per-module
callables or a per-module index into a table. This is a property of the
software contract and not of the physics, and it is listed again in
@sec-optical-module-validity so that it is not mistaken for one.

## The discrete algorithm {#sec-optical-module-algorithm}

What `DetectorArray` does on construction and on use:

1. **Check the shapes.** `positions_m` and `orientations` must both be finite
   $(N,3)$ arrays with $N\ge1$ and matching shapes.
2. **Normalise the orientations.** Non-zero vectors are divided by their norms,
   so $\hat{\mathbf o}_d$ is a unit vector whatever the user supplied. A zero
   orientation is rejected.
3. **Broadcast the area.** A scalar `effective_area_m2` is expanded to one
   value per module; an array must have one value per module.
4. **Check the area.** Every value must be finite and strictly positive.
5. **Check the identifiers.** Each identifier array must carry exactly one
   entry per module.
6. **Probe the angular response** on a set of cosines spanning $[-1,1]$ and
   require the returned values to be finite, non-negative, and of the same
   shape as the input.
7. **Probe the spectral response** at a few wavelengths with the same
   requirements.
8. **Re-check on use.** `spectral_weight` verifies finiteness and
   non-negativity again at every call, because the probe at construction sampled
   a handful of points and the real call may ask for others.
9. **Measure the bandwidth only when needed.** The Legendre coefficients and
   $L_A$ are computed when a transport kernel asks for them, not at
   construction. `acceptance_coefficients` evaluates the angular callable again
   on its quadrature nodes and rejects negative or non-finite values there; the
   result is cached on the kernel because the shape is common to the whole
   array. The convenience method `angular_weight` itself performs no such
   second validation, so a caller using it directly remains responsible for the
   values returned away from the construction probe.

Steps 6 and 7 deserve a caveat rather than confidence. A probe on a fixed grid
of cosines and a few wavelengths is a smoke test: it catches a sign error or a
function that returns the wrong shape, and it cannot prove that a user callable
is finite and non-negative everywhere on its domain. The spectral route checks
again at every use; the transport route checks the angular function again when
it constructs its Legendre coefficients. A direct call to `angular_weight`
does not.

## Correspondence with the code {#sec-optical-module-code}

| Mathematics | Symbol |
|:--|:--|
| $\mathbf x_d$, $\hat{\mathbf o}_d$, $S_d$, $\mathcal A$, $\epsilon$ | `lighthit.model.DetectorArray` |
| $c$ for a point source, @eq-module-head-on-cosine | `lighthit.model.DetectorArray.head_on_cosine` |
| $\mathcal A(c)$ for a point source | `lighthit.model.DetectorArray.angular_weight` |
| $\epsilon(\lambda)$, re-checked at the call | `lighthit.model.DetectorArray.spectral_weight` |
| $\alpha_\ell$, @eq-acceptance-coefficients | `lighthit.cache.acceptance_coefficients` |
| $\mathcal A\equiv1$, @eq-acceptance-isotropic | `lighthit.cache.isotropic_acceptance` |
| $L_A$ and the residual above it | `lighthit.directional.acceptance_bandwidth` |
| The module model chosen for a run | `lighthit.transport.TransportKernel.acceptance` |
| $N_{db}$ and $Q_d$ | `lighthit.transport.TransportResponse` |

One remark. `TransportKernel.acceptance` is where the refusal described in
@sec-optical-module-legendre actually happens: it measures the bandwidth, and
if the coefficients are still above tolerance at the top of the probed range it
stops with an error naming the clipped-response case, unless the configuration
states a truncation degree explicitly. The measurement is cached on the kernel
because @eq-acceptance-coefficients depends on the shape of $\mathcal A$ and on
nothing else --- not on the module, not on its orientation, not on the
wavelength.

## A worked number {#sec-optical-module-example}

Public synthetic parameters only, no transport solve and no cache. Reproduce
with

```bash
OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1 \
NUMBA_NUM_THREADS=1 \
  python scripts/run_optical_module_example.py --output .build/optical-module-example
```

The stored output is `docs/optical-module-example/summary.json`, which carries
the configuration, the library versions, the thread settings and every boolean
check beside the numbers below.

**Geometry.** A point source at the origin and three identical modules 30 m
away, differing only in where they look.

| Module | position, m | $\hat{\mathbf o}_d$ | $c$ | $\mathcal A(c)$ |
|:--|:--|:--|--:|--:|
| head-on | $(0,0,-30)$ | $(0,0,1)$ | $+1$ | $1.00$ |
| side-on | $(30,0,0)$ | $(0,1,0)$ | $0$ | $0.40$ |
| back-on | $(0,0,30)$ | $(0,0,1)$ | $-1$ | $0.04$ |

The acceptance is the quadratic $\mathcal A(c)=0.40+0.48c+0.12c^2$, which is
positive on the whole interval --- $\mathcal A(-1)=0.04$, not zero --- so it
needs no clipping and is band-limited exactly at degree 2. The three cosines
come out as $+1$, $0$, $-1$ to within $10^{-15}$.

**Expected photoelectrons.** Take a known monochromatic fluence of
$F=1000$ photons per square metre at 450 nm incident along the line from the
source, a reference area $S_d=0.05\ \mathrm m^2$ and a flat
$\epsilon=0.2$. These are choices of this example: the package fixes no value
for either, and where $F$ comes from is the business of @sec-scattering-orders
and @sec-time-and-bins. Then $N_d=S_d\,\epsilon\,\mathcal A(c_d)\,F$ gives

| Module | $N_d$, p.e. |
|:--|--:|
| head-on | $10.0$ |
| side-on | $4.0$ |
| back-on | $0.4$ |

A factor of 25 between the head-on and back-on module, from the acceptance
alone, at the same distance and with the same area and efficiency.

**The Legendre coefficients.** Measured with a 2048-node rule,
$$
\alpha_0=5.5292031,\quad \alpha_1=2.0106193,\quad \alpha_2=0.2010619,
$$
which analytically equal $2\pi\cdot0.88$, $2\pi\cdot0.32$ and
$2\pi\cdot0.032$. The script requires their relative error, every coefficient
above degree 2 relative to the peak, and the reconstruction error on 401 points
all to stay below $10^{-10}$. It measures $L_A=2$. The isotropic acceptance is
checked against $\alpha_0=4\pi$ with the same $10^{-10}$ bound on every higher
coefficient. Exact floating-point residuals are recorded only in the JSON,
because they change with the quadrature implementation and library version.

**A response that is not band-limited.** Replace the quadratic by
$\max(0,\,0.2+0.9c)$, which is clipped below $c=-2/9$. Its coefficients do not
terminate:

| $\ell$ | 3 | 8 | 16 | 32 | 64 |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| $\lvert\alpha_\ell\rvert/\alpha_{\rm peak}$ | $3.4\times10^{-2}$ | $1.4\times10^{-3}$ | $8.1\times10^{-4}$ | $9.4\times10^{-5}$ | $9.4\times10^{-6}$ |

They fall off, but algebraically: between degree 32 and degree 64 the envelope
drops by a factor of ten, a local exponent of $3.3$. The coefficients also
oscillate, so a slope read between two degrees indicates the envelope and
proves no power law. Probed to degree 64 the measured bandwidth comes back as
64 --- the top of the range --- which says only that the response is **not**
band-limited inside the range probed. It does not measure an infinite
bandwidth, and no probe of finite extent could.

## Checks {#sec-optical-module-checks}

Sixteen checks are recorded as booleans in the stored summary and the script
exits with a failure if any is false.

**Geometry and sign.** The stored orientations are unit vectors to
$10^{-15}$, and the head-on, side-on and back-on cosines are $+1$, $0$, $-1$ to
the same level. This is the check that the sign convention of
@eq-module-orientation is the one the code implements; an inverted convention
would return $-1$, $0$, $+1$ and the acceptance values would swap.

**Response values.** $\mathcal A$ at those three cosines is $1$, $0.4$, $0.04$
to $10^{-15}$, matching the quadratic evaluated by hand.

**Coefficients against the analytic values.** $\alpha_0,\alpha_1,\alpha_2$
are compared with $2\pi(0.88,\,0.32,\,0.032)$, computed by hand from the
quadratic, and everything above degree 2 is compared with zero relative to the
peak. The script requires both errors to stay below $10^{-10}$. The stored JSON
keeps the actual residuals together with the environment that produced them;
the prose does not promote those backend-dependent last digits to physical
results.

**Reconstruction.** @eq-acceptance-series truncated at $L_A=2$ must reproduce
$\mathcal A$ across $[-1,1]$ with maximum error below $10^{-10}$, which tests
the normalisation $(2\ell+1)/4\pi$ and not only the coefficients.

**The isotropic limit.** $\mathcal A\equiv1$ is required to give
$\alpha_0=4\pi$ and every higher coefficient below $10^{-10}$ of the peak.

**Linearity.** Doubling $S_d$ doubles every $N_d$ and halving $\epsilon$ halves
every $N_d$, both to zero error. @eq-module-factorisation is a product, and
this is what makes the scale degeneracy of
@sec-optical-module-assumptions real rather than hypothetical: these three
checks cannot tell which factor carries the normalisation.

**The contract refuses bad responses.** An angular response that goes negative
and a spectral response that goes negative are both rejected at construction
with `detector response functions must return finite nonnegative arrays`, and
@eq-acceptance-coefficients refuses a negative acceptance separately with
`acceptance must be nonnegative`.

**The clipped response is caught.** Its largest relative coefficient above
degree 2 is $3.4\times10^{-2}$, four orders above the corresponding number for
the quadratic, and the bandwidth probe saturates. Nothing here is silent.

Every number above is a check of this chapter's model against arithmetic or
against a hand calculation. None of it validates the *transport* that supplies
$I_\lambda$ to @eq-module-rate; that is the business of later chapters.

## Range of validity {#sec-optical-module-validity}

- **The module is a point.** It has a reference area but no surface, no
  extent and no orientation-dependent geometrical cross-section.
- **The acceptance is axially symmetric.** $\mathcal A$ depends on one cosine,
  so a module with an azimuthal structure about its own axis is not
  representable.
- **The response shape is shared.** One `angular_acceptance` and one
  `spectral_efficiency` per `DetectorArray`; modules with different shapes need
  separate arrays or an extended contract (@sec-optical-module-shared).
- **No glass and no ray tracing.** There is no sphere to intersect, no
  refraction at an interface and no photon path inside the module. Transmission
  and reflection enter only through the numbers the user puts into
  $\epsilon(\lambda)$ and $\mathcal A(c)$.
- **No shadowing.** A string, a cable, a neighbouring module or any other
  structure between the light and the module is not modelled.
- **No readout.** No saturation, no transit-time spread beyond an optional
  Gaussian smearing applied afterwards, no electronics, no trigger, no noise.
- **The response is linear and returns an expectation.** Doubling the incident
  light doubles $N_{db}$; nothing here carries a fluctuation.
- **The absolute normalisation is the user's to keep consistent.** It is spread
  across $S_d$, $\epsilon$ and $\mathcal A$, and the package checks none of the
  three against the others.

## Exercises {#sec-optical-module-exercises}

1. Verify the units of @eq-module-rate and @eq-module-bin term by term,
   starting from the definition of $I_\lambda$ in @eq-spectral-intensity, and
   state where the photon-to-photoelectron conversion enters.
2. Derive the three cosines of @sec-optical-module-example directly from
   @eq-module-cosine, using the travel direction of the unscattered photon, and
   confirm that @eq-module-head-on-cosine gives the same three numbers.
3. Compute $\alpha_0$, $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ by hand for
   $\mathcal A(c)=0.40+0.48c+0.12c^2$ and show that every higher coefficient
   vanishes identically.
4. Prove @eq-acceptance-isotropic from @eq-acceptance-coefficients using the
   orthogonality of the Legendre polynomials, and say why $4\pi$ rather than
   $1$ is the natural normalisation for $\alpha_0$.
5. Show that $(S_d,\epsilon,\mathcal A)\to(kS_d,\epsilon/k,\mathcal A)$ and
   $(S_d,\epsilon,\mathcal A)\to(S_d,k\epsilon,\mathcal A/k)$ leave every
   $N_{db}$ unchanged. Then say which of the three factors you would fix by
   convention, and what the other two must then mean.
6. Explain why $\max(0,\,0.2+0.9c)$ has coefficients that fall off
   algebraically rather than terminating, in terms of the smoothness of the
   function at $c=-2/9$. Predict how the exponent changes if the clipping is
   replaced by a smooth roll-off with a continuous first derivative, and test
   the prediction numerically.
7. Explain why the centroid cosine is exact for the unscattered term and
   insufficient for scattered light. Construct an intensity field at a module
   for which the two differ by more than a factor of two.
8. Propose an extension of the `DetectorArray` contract that admits modules
   with different angular shapes in one array. Say what it costs: which
   quantities that are now computed once per array would have to be computed
   once per shape, and which per module.
